text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London retreated slightly from their fresh surge at the close as some speculators who bought early ahead of New York sold back in the afternoon. But prices still finished the day higher, with benchmark May holding above the $1,610 per tonne level.

Fund and trade buying took the front-month to its intraday peak of $1,650, the highest in two weeks, after news of a smaller than expected rise in the US March green coffee stocks. London's May closed $37 up at $1,615 per tonne while most-active July was $35 firmer at $1,630 per tonne but below its intraday high of $1,668. Despite the rise, robustas continued to trail arabica prices, with the May/May arbitrage holding at a wide 134 cents.

Arabica futures in New York charged higher, with spot May ending at more than a two-and-a-half-year high as speculators bought heavily after a monthly report showed a much lower than expected rise in consumer coffee stocks. May futures surged to a new life of contract high of 213.00 cents/lb during the day, but traders said a round of profit taking and producer selling trimmed gains. May delivery finished at 208.05 cents/lb, the highest level on the weekly charts since September 1994, up 15.65 cents/lb - or eight per cent - on the day.

Second month July soared 10.65 cents/lb to 185.30 cents/lb, while the back months closed up 6.00 to 8.25. The May/July switch, a barometer of nearby availability, ballooned to 22.75 cents, up from 17.75 cents at the close on Tuesday. But while bullish technical and fundamentals could lead to further gains, some traders warned that soaring futures prices could prompt roasters to raise retail prices again, which could hurt consumption.
After Wednesday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks were down 750 60-kg bags, to 80,078 bags as of April 15. There were no bags pending grading, the exchange said.

BRAZIL - Two key coffee ports after Santos are expected be hit by a 48-hour national strike by stevedores due to begin at 0700 local/1000 GMT Friday after union officials in Rio de Janeiro and Vitoria said they were going to take part in the work stoppage. Of the 1.53 mn bags of coffee exported during March, 1.15 mn bags were shipped from Santos, just under 300,000 bags from Vitoria and around 72,000 bags from Rio de Janeiro.

The remaining coffee was shipped from Paranagua, Varginha and Salvador. So far this month, most coffee has been shipped from Santos which has handled 279,148 out of a total 300,257 bags loaded by April 14, according to the Rio de Janeiro Coffee Bulletin. Expectations for total shipments in April are of a similar size to March with April export registrations to March 28 covering 1.58 mn bags.

BRAZIL - Espirito Santo state should produce 3.38 mn 60-kg bags of coffee in 1997/98, down from a previous estimate of 3.59 mn bags released in December, according to the state agricultural secretariat. The forecast is down almost 32 per cent on the 4.97 mn bags produced in 1996/97, it was added. Out of the total arabica coffee is now expected to account for 900,000 bags against the previous forecast of 1.06 mn bags.

Conillon coffee production is estimated at 2.48 mn bags, down from 2.53 mn estimated earlier. Production of arabica and robusta coffee in 1996/97 was 1.69 mn and 3.28 mn bags respectively. The fall in output is due to the on-off cycle particularly in arabica coffee which sees a smaller crop every other year, said Marcos Moulin, agronomist at the department responsible for the state's crop estimates. In addition the late arrival of rains hit bean-setting this year which has only become apparent in the last few months.

COSTA RICA - Costa Rica ended its 1996/97 coffee campaign with a crop of 2.7 mn 60-kg bags, similar to last cycle, the executive director of the Costa Rican Coffee Institute said. Guillermo Canet told Reuters that exports to April 7 had totalled 1.533 mn bags. He said available exportable production from this cycle was around 700,000 bags and the remainder would go for internal consumption.

It appears that fears that the Costa Rican harvest would drop to 2.3 mn bags never materialized. The institute predicted in January that output would fall because of a cyclical dip and damage from Hurricane Cesar last autumn. Canet said for the 1997/98 crop the preliminary forecast was for another 2.7 mn bags crop.
